title: Derivatives of exp, log, trig, inverse trig
examples: How do I find the derivative of the natural logarithm of a cosine function?
Can you show me another example using the chain rule with exponential functions?
What is the derivative of the inverse sine function multiplied by x?

explain.say: Today we look at derivatives of common functions. We will use the chain rule often. Remember the chain rule is essential for these problems.

draw.text: Derivatives of exp, log, trig, inverse trig

explain.say: First, we review the basic derivatives. The derivative of the natural logarithm of x is simply one over x. The derivative of the exponential function e to the x is also e to the x.
Next, let us look at the chain rule. If you have a function inside another function, you must differentiate from the outside in. You multiply by the derivative of the inside part.

Now we combine these ideas. To differentiate ln of cosine x, we treat cosine x as the inside function. We take one over the inside, times the derivative of cosine x. This gives us one over cosine x times negative sine x.

items: Treat cos x as inside function

faq.q: What is the derivative of ln of x squared plus one?
faq.a: You use the chain rule here. The derivative is one over x squared plus one, multiplied by the derivative of x squared plus one. The derivative is two x, so the result is two x over x squared plus one.
asks: What is the derivative of the natural log of a quadratic?

faq.q: When do I use the chain rule with trigonometric functions?
faq.a: You use it any time a trig function has an inner function. For example, differentiating sine of three x requires multiplying by the derivative of three x, which is three.
asks: Do I always use the chain rule with trig functions?
What if the argument of sine is not just x?

faq.q: Is the derivative of e to the sine x just e to the sine x?
faq.a: No, you must use the chain rule. The derivative is e to the sine x, multiplied by the derivative of sine x. This equals e to the sine x times cosine x.
asks: How do I differentiate e^(sin x)?
Does the chain rule apply to e to trig functions?

faq.q: What is the derivative of the inverse cosine of x?
faq.a: The derivative of arccosine x is negative one over the square root of one minus x squared. This is a standard result you should memorize.
asks: What is the derivative of arccos(x)?
Can I use the chain rule on arccos?

faq.q: If I have ln(e x), do I need the chain rule?
faq.a: You can simplify this first. ln(e x) is the same as ln(e) plus ln(x). Since ln(e) is one, the derivative is just one plus one over x.
asks: Is ln(e x) different from ln(e) + ln(x)?
How do I differentiate ln(e x)?

facts: The derivative of the natural logarithm of x is one over x.
The derivative of e to x is e to x.
The derivative of sine x is cosine x.
The derivative of cosine x is negative sine x.

quiz.why: You can use the property that ln(a x) equals ln(a) plus ln(x). Since ln(a) is a constant, its derivative is zero. Thus, the derivative is zero plus one over x.

wrong.1: This mistake happens when you incorrectly apply the constant multiple rule to the argument.
wrong.2: This incorrectly treats the constant three as needing to be multiplied by the derivative of the function.
wrong.3: This confuses the derivative with simply multiplying the constant by the original function.

quiz.why: This requires the chain rule. You differentiate the outside, e to something, giving e to x squared. Then you multiply by the derivative of the inside, x squared, which is two x.

wrong.0: This incorrectly substitutes x for x squared in the exponent of the final result.
wrong.1: This incorrectly applies the power rule to the exponent instead of using the chain rule.
wrong.3: This forgets to multiply by the derivative of the inner function, x squared.

quiz.say: What is the derivative of cos(5x)?
quiz.why: Using the chain rule, the derivative of cosine is negative sine. You must multiply this by the derivative of the inside, five x, which is five. So, negative sine times five.

wrong.0: This forgets to multiply by the derivative of the inner function, five x.
wrong.1: This incorrectly assumes the derivative of cosine is itself, ignoring the chain rule.
wrong.2: This incorrectly applies the power rule to the cosine function itself.
